claims.claim: Ucn expression was shifted, reaching farther into the lateral LSO in deaf animals compared to hearing controls.
claims.source: Ucn expression was also shifted, reaching farther into the lateral LSO in deaf animals compared to hearing controls (Figure 7H and M, Figure 7—figure supplement 1I; n=7 control LSOs from 4 animals, 9 Tmc1/2dKO LSOs from 5 animals).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7H and M.

claims.claim: The fraction of ChAT+ LOCs expressing TH was elevated 9 days after sound exposure.
claims.source: As expected, the fraction of ChAT+ LOCs expressing TH was elevated 9 days after sound exposure (Figure 8A–C; n=4 exposed and 4 unexposed animals of either sex).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A-C.

claims.claim: An even larger increase in the fraction of LOCs expressing Ucn or NPY was observed after sound exposure.
claims.source: In addition, we observed an even larger increase in the fraction of LOCs expressing Ucn or NPY (Figure 8A and D–G).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A and D-G.

claims.claim: The levels of CGRP increased qualitatively throughout the LSO after sound exposure.
claims.source: Because all LOCs already express CGRP, there was no increase in the fraction of CGRP+ LOCs, although the levels of CGRP increased qualitatively throughout the LSO (Figure 8A, H, I).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A, H, and I.

claims.claim: The slope of peptide expression remained unaltered after sound exposure, with higher levels largely constrained to the medial wing.
claims.source: Across all neuropeptides, the slope of peptide expression remained unaltered after sound exposure, with higher levels largely constrained to the medial wing (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: TH levels increased throughout the LSO after sound exposure.
claims.source: In contrast, TH levels increased throughout the LSO, suggesting that the mechanisms driving LOCs to express TH may be different from those that govern neuropeptide expression (Figure 8A–C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A-C.

claims.claim: Hearing shapes the signaling repertoire of a subset of LOC neurons, both developmentally and in adults.
claims.source: Thus, hearing shapes the signaling repertoire of a subset of LOC neurons, both developmentally and in adults.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the developmental and sound exposure experiments.

claims.claim: Some variant of the olivocochlear efferent system exists for all hair cell sensory systems.
claims.source: Some variant of the olivocochlear efferent system exists for all hair cell sensory systems: groups of feedback cells project to auditory, vestibular, and lateral line neurons in all classes of vertebrates, and even some invertebrates (Roberts and Meredith, 1992).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The wide conservation of the olivocochlear system across evolutionary time suggests that OCNs play a crucial functional role.
claims.source: The wide conservation of this circuitry across evolutionary time suggests that OCNs play a crucial functional role.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary conservation.

claims.claim: Induced peptide expression persists for over a week after noise exposure.
claims.source: Induced peptide expression persists for over a week after noise exposure (Figure 8), presenting a mechanism by which LOCs can modulate downstream targets on the timescale of days.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8, which examines expression 9 days after exposure.

claims.claim: LOC1s and LOC2s vary in expression of genes that encode transcription factors and cell-adhesion molecules.
claims.source: First, LOC1s and LOC2s vary in expression of genes that encode transcription factors and cell-adhesion molecules, attributes that are typically associated with cell types rather than cell states (Paul et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the differential expression analysis and a citation.

claims.claim: Peptide-high LOC2s are anatomically segregated from LOC1s.
claims.source: Second, peptide-high LOC2s are anatomically segregated from LOC1s (Figure 3O, P).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3O and P.

claims.claim: The medial bias in neuropeptide expression is already present by at least P5/P6, prior to the onset of hearing.
claims.source: Moreover, the medial bias in neuropeptide expression is already present by at least P5/P6, prior to the onset of hearing, suggesting that this effect cannot be attributed to a stimulus that might preferentially activate medial LOCs, like ultrasonic vocalizations (Figure 7E, F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E and F.

claims.claim: NPY-expressing cells are biased to the medial LSO across perturbations, whereas cells in the far lateral LSO never express Ucn or NPY.
claims.source: Finally, although we also show that peptide expression in LOCs can be altered by sound (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Figure 8), NPY-expressing cells are biased to the medial LSO across perturbations, whereas cells in the far lateral LSO never express Ucn or NPY (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is shown across multiple figures examining different conditions.

claims.claim: Ucn and CGRP are enriched in the medial LSO of mature gerbils and rats, respectively.
claims.source: Although LOC2s have never been specifically described in the literature, Ucn and CGRP are also enriched in the medial LSO of mature gerbils and rats, respectively, indicating that LOC1/2 differences may be conserved across species (Kaiser et al., 2011; Vetter et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in other species.

claims.claim: Bifurcating axons did not differ from non-bifurcating axons in any anatomical metric examined.
claims.source: Nevertheless, although we cannot be certain whether any individual LOC axons in our 3D reconstructions arise from shell or intrinsic neurons, we found that bifurcating axons—a putative marker of shell neuron identity (Warr et al., 1997)—did not differ from non-bifurcating axons in any anatomical metric we examined (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–N), indicating that the distinction between shell and intrinsic LOCs does not explain the diversity of LOC morphology present in mice.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J-N.

claims.claim: The distinction between LOC1s and LOC2s is insufficient to explain LOC heterogeneity.
claims.source: The distinction between LOC1s and LOC2s is also insufficient to explain LOC heterogeneity: we found no meaningful correlations between the fraction of NPY+ pre-synaptic puncta in LOC axons and any morphological attributes (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or between Calca-GFP intensity and any physiological characteristics (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the analyses in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: The molecular differences that define LOC2s do not correlate with any of the physiological or peripheral morphological characteristics measured.
claims.source: It is striking that the molecular differences that define LOC2s—as confirmed by in situ hybridization, immunostaining, and genetic labeling—do not correlate with any of the physiological or peripheral morphological characteristics that we measured.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: MOCs and LOCs can be molecularly distinguished by at least P1.
claims.source: Accordingly, MOCs and LOCs can be molecularly distinguished by at least P1, with many cell-type specific markers that persist into adulthood (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the developmental sequencing data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Both MOCs and LOCs downregulate several GABA receptor subunits while increasing expression of the glycine receptor subunit Glra1.
claims.source: For example, both MOCs and LOCs downregulate several GABA receptor subunits while increasing expression of the glycine receptor subunit Glra1, indicating a transition from receiving GABAergic to glycinergic inputs (Korada and Schwartz, 1999; Kotak et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the developmental gene expression data and supported by citations.

claims.claim: LOC2 specification may happen relatively early in development, as LOC2s can be recognized as early as P5 by enriched expression of NPY and CGRP in the medial LSO.
claims.source: As with diversification of broader OCN subtypes, LOC1/LOC2 specification may also happen relatively early in development, as LOC2s can be recognized as early as P5 by enriched expression of NPY and CGRP in the medial LSO (Figure 7E and F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E and F.

claims.claim: LOC2 markers such as NPY are localized medially both before and after the onset of hearing.
claims.source: In contrast, LOC2 markers such as NPY are localized medially both before and after the onset of hearing.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the developmental analysis in Figure 7.

claims.claim: LOCs express Hcrtr2, which encodes an orexin receptor.
claims.source: In keeping with this interpretation, LOCs, but not MOCs, express Hcrtr2, which encodes an orexin receptor (Figure 2Q), suggesting that LOCs may be poised to transmit information about general arousal state to the cochlea.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2Q.

claims.claim: The duration and intensity of sound exposure affect the number of LOCs that induce TH expression.
claims.source: Previous work found that the duration and intensity of sound exposure affect the number of LOCs that induce TH expression, with more intense stimuli inducing greater TH expression (Wu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from a citation.

claims.claim: Recordings from SGNs show that dopamine can reduce SGN firing rates.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, recordings from SGNs show that dopamine can reduce SGN firing rates, potentially as a way of reducing excitotoxicity evoked by loud sounds (Wu et al., 2020; Ruel et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Transcripts of the inhibitory, G-coupled NPY receptor Npy1r were detected in low levels in Type Ic SGNs.
claims.source: For example, transcripts of the inhibitory, G-coupled NPY receptor Npy1r were detected in low levels in Type Ic SGNs (Shrestha et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Most studies on the effects of CGRP in the inner ear of mammals or lateral line of amphibians have found that CGRP plays an excitatory role.
claims.source: Complicating this hypothesis, most studies on the effects of CGRP in the inner ear of mammals or lateral line of amphibians have found that CGRP plays an excitatory role (Bailey and Sewell, 2000a; Sewell and Starr, 1991; Bailey and Sewell, 2000b; Maison et al., 2003b; Le Prell et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Infusions of CGRP into the guinea pig cochlea increase the amplitude of compound action potentials (CAPs).
claims.source: Infusions of CGRP into the guinea pig cochlea increase the amplitude of compound action potentials (CAPs) (Le Prell et al., 2021)—a measure of bulk SGN activity—whereas CGRP knock-out mice exhibit decreased auditory brainstem response (ABR) amplitudes (Maison et al., 2003b), reinforcing the idea that CGRP enhances SGN firing.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The Ucn receptor Crhr1 is expressed in cochlear supporting cells.
claims.source: In support of this idea, the Ucn receptor Crhr1 is expressed in cochlear supporting cells, suggesting that they may be an alternate target of LOC signaling (Graham and Vetter, 2011; Liu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations.

claims.claim: NPY and CGRP are both immune-modulatory molecules that could alter inflammatory responses after acoustic injury.
claims.source: Immune cells are another possible target of LOC peptide release, as NPY and CGRP are both immune-modulatory molecules that could alter inflammatory responses after acoustic injury (Assas et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations.

results.result: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 45,828 cholinergic nuclei from the ventral brainstem across three developmental timepoints (P1, P5, P26-28) identified 56 clusters, with each neuronal cluster containing cells from all timepoints.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C13, C14, and C15 describe the sequencing methodology and dataset composition. The methods are clearly described, sample sizes are appropriate (61 animals), and quality control metrics are provided. The finding that clusters contain cells from all timepoints (C15) validates that clustering is not driven by batch effects.

results.result: OCN clusters were identified by Gata3 expression and distinguished into MOC and LOC subtypes using known markers (Ucn for LOCs, Atp1a3 for MOCs). A novel OCN marker, Cadps2, was identified and validated by FISH.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 establish OCN identity using established markers (Gata3, Ucn, Atp1a3) supported by citations and sequencing data. The novel marker Cadps2 is validated by both sequencing (C18) and orthogonal FISH experiments (C20, n=3 animals), providing converging evidence.

results.result: Novel stable markers distinguish LOCs (Col4a4) from MOCs (Zfp804a) across development. MOCs and LOCs express distinct cohorts of genes encoding transcription factors, adhesion molecules, and neurotransmitter receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 identify novel cell-type markers validated by FISH (Figure 2B-G). Claims C23-C25 demonstrate differential gene expression between subtypes using appropriate statistical methods (Wilcoxon rank-sum with Bonferroni correction). The findings are supported by violin plots and volcano plots showing clear separation.

results.result: Sub-clustering of mature OCNs revealed two LOC subtypes: LOC1 (242 cells) and LOC2 (75 cells). LOC2s are distinguished by neuropeptide expression (NPY, CGRP, Ucn, Calcb) and are anatomically restricted to the medial LSO.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 describe discovery of LOC2 subtype through sub-clustering analysis, differential expression analysis, and validation by immunostaining (Figure 3O, n=4 animals) and intersectional genetics (Figure 3P, n=4 animals). Multiple orthogonal approaches converge on the same conclusion. NPY is identified as the most reliable marker (C31).

results.result: Opioid peptide transcripts (Penk, Pdyn) were not detected in any LOC subtype by sequencing or FISH.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 reports negative findings for opioid peptides using both sequencing and FISH validation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H). This contradicts some prior literature claims but is supported by two independent methods. The negative result is appropriately reported.

results.result: NPY+ LOC2 axons span the entire base-to-apex length of the cochlea, though with decreasing density from base to apex.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C7 describe broad cochlear innervation by LOC2 axons using genetic labeling (NpyFlpO; ChatCre; Rosa26FLTG, n=10 animals). The finding is demonstrated in cochlear wholemounts (Figure 3Q) showing axons across all frequency regions despite density gradient.

results.result: Sparse genetic labeling using RetCreER revealed diverse MOC axon morphologies. 45% of MOC axons have synaptic puncta in the ISB, and individual MOCs can produce projections with variable morphologies and targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 describe MOC axon reconstruction using validated sparse labeling (n=40 axons from 9 animals). The approach is validated by consistency with prior dye-labeling studies (C36). Quantification shows no correlation between ISB innervation and other morphological features (C39), supporting the conclusion of individual MOC variability (C40).

results.result: LOC axons exhibit highly variable morphologies and connectivity patterns. Individual LOC axons contain both NPY+ and NPY- synaptic puncta distributed on both CALB2+ (pillar-side) and CALB2- (modiolar-side) SGN targets, with no correlation between NPY content and morphological features.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 describe LOC axon reconstructions (n=46 fibers from 9 animals) with detailed 3D analysis of NPY distribution and target selectivity. The lack of correlation between NPY status and multiple morphological metrics (C45, Figure 5P-U) is demonstrated through appropriate correlation analyses. The heterogeneity within individual axons (C42-C44) is well-documented.

results.result: Electrophysiological recordings from LOCs in Calca-GFP mice (P16-19) revealed no correlation between GFP intensity (peptide expression) and physiological properties including input resistance, membrane capacitance, or action potential characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 report electrophysiology from 20 animals with appropriate sample sizes. Multiple physiological parameters were tested (voltage-clamp and current-clamp), and none correlated with GFP intensity. Statistical analyses are appropriate (Pearson correlation, ANOVA). The negative result is striking but well-supported by comprehensive measurements.

results.result: Neuropeptide gene expression (Calca, Calcb, Ucn, NPY) increases in LOCs during postnatal development. Calca expression is spatially and temporally dynamic, showing low medial bias at P5/6, widespread expression at P12 (hearing onset), and medial restriction by P28.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55 describe developmental changes in peptide expression using sequencing data and FISH validation (2-3 animals per timepoint). The transient increase in Calca at hearing onset (C54) is clearly demonstrated in Figure 7F and is consistent with findings in other species (citations provided).

results.result: In congenitally deaf mice (Tmc1/2 double knockout), CGRP and Ucn expression gradients are perturbed after hearing onset, with high expression extending farther into the lateral LSO compared to hearing controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 demonstrate experience-dependent peptide expression using appropriate genetic model (Tmc1/2dKO, 4-6 animals per condition). Quantitative analysis of expression gradients shows significant differences after hearing onset (P27-28) but not before (P7-8), supporting activity-dependent regulation. Statistical tests are appropriate (Wilcoxon rank-sum).

results.result: Acoustic trauma (110 dB, 2 hours) induces sustained upregulation of neuropeptides (TH, NPY, Ucn, CGRP) in LOCs, persisting for at least 9 days. The spatial gradient of peptide expression is maintained, but TH increases throughout the LSO while neuropeptides remain medially biased.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64, C67 describe sound exposure effects (n=4 exposed and 4 unexposed animals). The upregulation of multiple peptides is demonstrated with appropriate quantification (fraction of expressing cells, intensity slopes). The differential spatial patterns between TH and neuropeptides (C62-C63) suggest distinct regulatory mechanisms. The 9-day timepoint demonstrates sustained expression (C67).

results.result: LOC1 and LOC2 represent distinct cell types rather than states, based on differential expression of transcription factors and adhesion molecules, anatomical segregation, early developmental specification (by P5/6), and conservation across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 provide multiple lines of evidence for LOC subtype identity: molecular differences in cell-type-associated genes (C68), anatomical segregation (C69), pre-hearing specification (C70), stability across perturbations (C71), and cross-species conservation (C72). The convergence of evidence from different approaches strongly supports the cell type vs. state distinction.

results.result: The distinction between LOC1 and LOC2 does not explain the full extent of LOC heterogeneity. Bifurcating vs. non-bifurcating axons show no morphological differences, and NPY expression does not correlate with physiological or morphological characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 report negative findings regarding LOC heterogeneity. The lack of correlation between shell/intrinsic identity (bifurcation) and morphology (C73) is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J-N. The disconnect between molecular identity and function (C74-C75) is demonstrated through comprehensive correlation analyses in Figures 5 and 6. These negative results are important for understanding LOC diversity.

results.result: MOCs and LOCs are molecularly distinct by P1, with developmental changes including downregulation of GABA receptor subunits and upregulation of glycine receptor Glra1, indicating a transition from GABAergic to glycinergic inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 describe early molecular divergence supported by sequencing data across timepoints (Figure 2). The developmental transition in receptor expression (C77) is consistent with known developmental changes in auditory circuits and is supported by citations. The findings establish early specification of OCN subtypes.

results.result: LOC2 specification occurs early in development, with enriched NPY and CGRP expression in the medial LSO detectable by P5, before and after hearing onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 demonstrate early LOC2 specification using developmental analysis (Figure 7E-F). The medial bias is present at P5/6 (pre-hearing) and persists through maturity, supporting early specification rather than activity-dependent induction of cell type identity.

results.result: LOCs express the orexin receptor Hcrtr2, suggesting they may transmit information about arousal state to the cochlea.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 identifies Hcrtr2 expression in LOCs but not MOCs (Figure 2Q). This is a descriptive finding supported by sequencing data. The functional interpretation about arousal is speculative but reasonable given the known role of orexin in arousal. The claim is appropriately framed as a suggestion.

results.result: OCNs are a small population of several hundred neurons in the SOC that project to the cochlea, enabling direct regulation of auditory processing and providing protection from sound-induced damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C12 describe established knowledge about OCN function, supported by historical citations (Rasmussen 1946, 1953) and illustrated in Figure 1A-B. These are background claims that provide context for the study and are well-established in the literature.

results.result: OCNs are poised to have diffuse, dynamic effects on auditory processing over timescales from milliseconds to days, and their evolutionary conservation suggests a crucial functional role.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C66 are integrative conclusions based on the combined findings of the study. C9 is supported by the demonstration of widespread anatomical projections (C7, C34) and sustained peptide upregulation after sound exposure (C67). C66 is an inference from evolutionary conservation (C65) that is reasonable but speculative. These are appropriate concluding statements.

results.result: Prior work has established that sound exposure induces TH expression in LOCs, dopamine reduces SGN firing, and various neuropeptide receptors are expressed in the cochlea, suggesting multiple potential mechanisms for LOC-mediated protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 summarize prior literature relevant to interpreting the current findings. Each claim is supported by appropriate citations. These are background claims that contextualize the discussion of potential functional roles for LOC neuropeptides. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.
